review_text_raw:
Tl;dr: game good. fake internet is fun to search and solve puzzles in. Minigames can be annoying, but are made up for by the unique style and strong storytelling.

What an incredibly unique and engaging game this is. I would normally advise anyone who is even a little interested to simply go in blind, but if you want a short description of the moment-to-moment: imagine a point and click adventure game, where you must locate certain information to progress, using internet search engines and personal e-mails as your setting.

If there is a flaw in the 7 hours/2 chapters that I've played, it's that sometimes you will be timed while searching for "key information" in a designated area. You often aren't told exactly what you're looking for, leading to, essentially, a pixel hunt where you sift through all the data as fast as you can, hoping you get lucky before time runs out. It's actually pretty effective at building tension, but failing often means a reset to a checkpoint that's JUST far back enough to be annoying, but not ruinous. Given this, for the love of all that's holy, leave the "hints" option turned on in settings. As far as I can tell, it doesn't hold your hand or spoil any deductions you need to make. It simply highlights relevant text when your mouse hovers over it, which I find invaluable.

Honestly, this hiccup is a small blemish on an otherwise fascinating and truly cool game. The gameplay is a form of social information gathering and hacking that I've never seen done in this way, nor organized as well as it is. You have all the info you need to deduce your next step at any time in your onscreen folder, and getting stuck, in my experience, is due to a lack of thoroughness on my part. Also, the stories really deliver some truly good gut-punches (again, of the two main chapters I've played). Maybe I'm a sap, but the conclusions always left me feeling bad, in the "best" way possible. On a related note, the translation is pretty solid. Some phrasing can come off as odd or unnatural, but the meaning of the sentence is never confused. Awkward from time to time, but perfectly understandable.

review_text_raw:
Cyber Manhunt, first episode is a 50/50 success, cautious positive recommendation here.

i obviously liked the game and finished it in the course of several days. Don't look too much at my game time, I often left the game running while attending some irl obligations.

I would like to first thank the dev for this game and for having taken the time to translate the game  (whatever may be the tools used for it) so we, non-chinese players, could venture into your universe. I've bought this game along with its DLC and the second game that is currently in Early access (I'll start that one when I've got some time).

But let's jump in the meat of the review. 

1)  I can't start without addressing the main issue of this game, for us non-chinese readers/speakers : the translation. Many things have been said about it and while the two DLC's do display a better text than the main game, let's be honest and say that it's the major con of the software. 

I would like to tone this concern down in regard with my earlier praise to the dev for translating it, but nonetheless it led me to check for guides on Steam and videos on youtube to solve some problems that were either due to a vague translation or to more problematic issues as I'll develop below.

2) Voice acting.... not necessary and not very welcome either. You've got a range of icons to tell us that we're listening to a phone call, it's not like we need to listen to anything in particular. Let's take the good examples of Orwell and Song of Farca that don't have any voice acting and yet have a great atmosphere, great writing, etc. And also, no option to mute voices only, Or you mute all the sounds (music being dealt with apart from it) or you have to listen to .... quite robotic or emotionless or otherwise misplayed dialogues. Again, DLC's level up the game a little more on that matter.

3) My main concern is definitely the lack of "respect" that I felt sometimes during the game. I understand that the dev team is very small, but then select what you display on screen, please. And make it, if not useful, at least usable. 
   - many web articles are just there for lore purpose, nothing else ;
   - tapped phone calls received through mail are not always usable to make the case progress ; 
   - some hinted leads are dead ends from the start, no way to investigate them ;
   - No way to direct call people we know the phone numbers.... ;
   - Sometimes, the chuncks of info that you have to select make little sense, mostly due to the translation. Why should I 
      select an obvious conclusion to a drama (for instance : "I'm alone in the world now that they're gone") and not the fact 
      themselves (for example : "They died in a car accident last month") ? ;
      Ok, it's not always that simplistic, but it's sometimes the case and in the end, it becomes more of a clicker game where 
      you hunt down info at random than an actual investigation. Again, respect your player intelligence or try to have a 
      better translated and adapted script, because while I'm grateful to you for your effort, it was a bit underwhelming...;
   - maybe my main grip here : you often have to select the information in a particular document and not anywhere else. 
      And that is a huge concern of mine. Let's say you see that NPC 1 got divorced while skimming through a web article. You could extract the data here and add it to the share folder, right ? No, you will have to wait for the same info to appear on an obscure Darknet-ish forum or on social medias, etc. Which is.... not unseen before but still annoying. 

Do respect your players. Be conscious of your own limitations and restrict our freedom of action right from the start instead of giving us the illusion of "freedom of action". Again, not unseen before in this kind of games and others genres. Indeed, it has been a recurring pattern since the beginning of gaming, but... maybe there are elegant ways to deal with it. Again, Orwell dealt with it quite nicely by focusing on what was relevant for us, for the story, for the game. Another thing that can be done is letting us "phone" the characters and just letting them or not answering, or blocking us, or just repeating the same automatic response. It would still tell us that it is a dead end, but at least we wouldn't feel like heavily disabled persons unable to put 2 and 2 and take action. 

4) Good writing, good story, good characters. I liked all the cases and the general story. Nothing new under the sky, but well done. The themes were indeed a bit stressful and character writing was deep enough for me to like/love/dislike/hate them and how corrupt or mischievous they can be. Good thriller all in all. Maybe the last DLC was a bit underwhelming. the tower-defence mini-game was interesting though !

5) Music, like voice acting, was a bit redundant, I quickly muted it and put my own in the background. The problem was the same with Song of Farca but at least you could change the track before muting it completely. Orwell did handle it better with a soft lift-like music. 


Ok, I talked too much.

TL;DR => buy it both because it's a good game and to support its dev(s). Despite the caveats I mentioned, I still mostly enjoyed my journey in this universe and will launch the second game when I get time. both gameplay DLC (the only paid DLC, that is) are of good value. "Home Sweet Home" being the better story-wise and the second DLC being better gameplay-wise (because of the mini tower-defence game ^^). 

Regards

review_text_raw:
The mechanics are that of an uninspired phishing simulation. Which contrasts with the narrative framing of "you are a really dangerous nerd". I feel like a game like grayhack or hacknet is fit more for that framing. Even the tutorial was highly boring for me. Maybe the story you get after the tutorial is good, but i didn't get that far.

Well you see I understand that a game would need some embellishing and effects to sell the power fantasy and divert from the seams of skipping real life logic, but the choices this game made regarding that front makes me see those seams harder rather than immersing me in the fantasy.

very light spoilers ahead from the first ten minutes of gameplay(tutorial and intro)

First, i got whiplashed right off with the phrase "our company got a BILLION BYTES of customer data". Holy shit dude, that's a lot for a large tech company at the like 90s maybe. Not for the presented "everyone is glued to their phones using social media" setting.  Less than a god damn gigabyte, basically three times less than the space this game takes on your ssd.

Then we got the random code prompts opening every time we copy the details from the browser about someone's facebook account to some contacts type information collection software. It feels less hackery and more like the "linux users when x" memes, because why would code prompts open when you are just copy pasting something from one gui to some other gui.


Then apparently we have access to the data of almost all citizens in our nation through the company database software. For some reason when accessing the data we or the software executes almost totally unrelated linux commands, which i don't understand why since it is not a cli tool but poses as a professional corpo gui software, but i guess the company in the story fired the user interface designer/programmer before they finished their job.

Then there is the password "cracker" software. Except this game's version makes me feel like a loser script kiddie the most. All you do is fill in a bunch of details you gathered from the dude's social media page, and the "cracker" spits out some password guess with very few amount of characters based on the entered information. And somehow it's correct like it's some oracle.

It reminds me of that one CheeseParade skit where the guy goes "He's not a hacker, he's a password guesser", and then the guy proceeds to get locked out of the system for inputting the wrong password since it was a guess based on a whim.

Also the OS apparently can't handle a bunch of high speed showcase of cyber security news, crashes and has to restart, which felt like a funny unintentional commentary on the ram shortage crisis. That was the most fun part of the game for me. 

Anyways, so if you like an overly dressed up phishing simulator with seemingly nice worldbuilding and perhaps a good story if you ignore the technical knowledge shortcomings of the writers here and there, maybe its your thing, Otherwise, nah.

review_text_raw:
The execution needs work. 

I enjoy Orwell and other games in this vein. My main issue here is that it's tedious. It doesn't show you which information it wants you to click on until you mouse over it. But sometimes clearly important information isn't clickable. Other times information will be essential to click, but it's unclear exactly why. The result is that you have to mouse over everything, relevant or not. If you missed something, you have to search everywhere again to find it. 

The result was me being in a place where I knew all the answers and had solved everything, but wasn't allowed to end the level because I had missed clicking on some piece of information somewhere. I looked at important pieces of information multiple times, and eventually found that the piece I had missed was something that was only slightly relevant to the situation at hand. 

In other words- it didn't make me feel like I was solving puzzles. It made me feel like I was trying every single option whether it made sense or not, because that was the only way to progress. When I got stuck, it wasn't because I couldn't figure something out or because I didn't understand, it was because there was some random thing that I hadn't realized it wanted me to do.

review_text_raw:
This game has a couple of problems:
1. Some of the things you have to deduce are really far fetched. Like:
[spoiler]You're supposed to figure out which limb a person has injured by assuming that all people are right handed[/spoiler]. I needed to look that up, after like 20 minutes.
2. To get the achievement for each chapter you have to get all the evidence and the only way to get evidence is to hover over every text, because if it is evidence it will be marked red. This can be turned of in the settings, but that just makes it even harder!
3. While doing a dialogue you may need to know things along the lines of 'when does this person do x?' and you can't look it up while doing the dialogue which mean it's basically 'choose something random; it's the wrong choice; look it up; advance dialogue; repeat'. I'm sorry but it can't remember every minute detail that may or may not be relevant in a dialogue tree, 30 minutes down the line.
4. QoL features I wish the game had. These are not really a problem but would be nice:
  - The back, forward and reload buttons in the browser don't work.
  - You can't enter URLs in the browser
  - Sometimes the browser opens new tabs, sometimes it doesn't. Would be nice if 'new tab' was bound to middle mouse button and 'open here' to left click.
  - The password cracker, which seems to be made to be like a dictionary attack thingie, doesn't crack the password unless it has ALL information even if the information isn't contained in the password e.g. 
  "Name: Susi"
  "Date of birth: 1.1.1970"
  resulting password is '111970"
  It wouldn't need the name for that.
  - Sometimes text messages appear on both sides of account and sometimes they're only on one side e.g.
  You lock into Alice's and Bob's account and on Alice's account the conversation is
  A: "Hi long time no see"
  B: "Are you ghosting me?"
  
  And on Bob's account it's
  A: "Hi long time no see"
  B: "Are you ghosting me?"
  one day later
  B: "Sorry. Didn't see your messages. Here's the super secret info you need."
  A: "Thank you"
  - Calling a person before you're supposed to just tells you that they're not available currently.
  - Hacking things is less like a puzzle and more of 'type this into a text box, then you have 5 minutes to find what you want and if you don't succeed you restart and have to type the text into the box again'. Like it's actually type a text into a box. It's 'this is the password `ERGT467´ type this into the text box below'. The time limit just seems pointless and the having to repeat everything after you run out of time seems frustrating.

review_text_raw:
I give Cyber Manhunt a middle B. It's a fun investigation game that is similar to Orwell and Analogue: A Hate Story where you piece together the plot by using "hacking," or really Hollywood-style hacking in between social engineering.

The gameplay suffers a bit for its loop, in which the majority of your time is spent looking through in-game social media logs of your subjects. That's a fun premise, but the game proceeds by having you click on relevant lines of text. When you hover your cursor over lines you can "collect" to add to your case file, the lines turn red, but otherwise there is no indication which bits are relevant. There are many times early on I just missed the lines in question, and so I spent the last few chapter meticulously mousing over EVERYTHING so I didn't miss anything, but I STILL missed things. It was a little frustrating and I had to use a guide a couple times to find what I had overlooked, even though I read everything.

More frustrating than that though are the mini-games. Usually when doing something more intense than reading, you're playing a mini-game to hack a system or reason out a situation. For the most part these mini-games aren't difficult and I appreciate the variety. However, in later chapters the mini-games start getting time limits, and some of these are unnecessarily harsh. A particular hacking mini-game in Chapter 5 nearly made me rage quit, and even with a video tutorial from YouTube, I was really struggling to get past it. Maybe I'm just a slow reader, but I think it's just less-than-good game design.

The developer seemed to understand those criticisms too because in the Home Sweet Home DLC there aren't any time limits, and in Hello World there is only one mini-game with a time limit that's [i]incredibly[/i] generous. Also in the DLCs, the mini-games can be straight up skipped. I wish that had been in the base game.

Luckily, all mini-games and gameplay loop tedium are absolutely overshadowed by the excellent story. All seven chapters (DLC included) had great twists and turns. All the cases are connected in subtle ways, and almost no one ended up how they began. All the characters were complex, and the writers absolutely nailed social media posts, including strangers of all genders uncomfortably randomly hitting on strangers in their own feeds. And what starts off as a "simple" matter of investigation eventually spirals into sci-fi and metaphysical questions. I loved it.

The English translation is unfortunately wonky, and there are typos or "just doesn't sound right" issues in just about every other sentence. There's also some polish issues where the voice acting doesn't quite match up with what's on the screen, like the script changed after the line were recorded. Even so, the translation is good enough that you can follow what's going on and there's nothing more egregious than mixing up pronouns. But man, if the story had been run through a native English speaker/writer before being released, this would have been an [i]incredible[/i] story.

The music is awesome as well, and really sets the mood, but the story really caries the game. I'm excited to try the sequel now, though I'm hoping the gameplay loop for Cyber Manhunt 2 is less tedious.

The developer seemed to understand those criticisms too because in the Home Sweet Home DLC there aren't any time limits, and in Hello World there is only one mini-game with a time limit that's [i]incredibly[/i] generous. Also in the DLCs, the mini-games can be straight up skipped. I wish that had been in the base game. Luckily, all mini-games and gameplay loop tedium are absolutely overshadowed by the excellent story. All seven chapters (DLC included) had great twists and turns. All the cases are connected in subtle ways, and almost no one ended up how they began. All the characters were complex, and the writers absolutely nailed social media posts, including strangers of all genders uncomfortably randomly hitting on strangers in their own feeds. And what starts off as a "simple" matter of investigation eventually spirals into sci-fi and metaphysical questions. I loved it. The English translation is unfortunately wonky, and there are typos or "just doesn't sound right" issues in just about every other sentence. There's also some polish issues where the voice acting doesn't quite match up with what's on the screen, like the script changed after the line were recorded. Even so, the translation is good enough that you can follow what's going on and there's nothing more egregious than mixing up pronouns. But man, if the story had been run through a native English speaker/writer before being released, this would have been an [i]incredible[/i] story. The music is awesome as well, and really sets the mood, but the story really caries the game. I'm excited to try the sequel now, though I'm hoping the gameplay loop for Cyber Manhunt 2 is less tedious.

- hacking passwords: copy/paste info from another window and click the button
- phishing: you have to trial and error until you find the random sequence they imagined
Aside from that, getting into emails and other accounts, all gets repetitive really fast. 
About translations: I read about other reviewers complaining about the English. When I purchased the game they had just released improved translations, but there is still much work to do...
Last point: what I would have liked to see, is a much more open gameplay, where one has to read everything to find clues, take their own notes, and has chances to make mistakes so that there is at least an illusion that the path to success isn't linear.

TL;DR: What it lacks in interesting mechanics it makes up for in repetetiveness.

Slightly longer review: 

You google names, go to their facebook page, click on interesting info and then google that, or enter it into the same five programs while the UI makes you wait for 10 seconds every time you found a hint. Then you answer some exams to check if you paid attention. If you expect deductions or logic puzzles, you will not find those here. It is all simply about reading and remembering information.

Sometimes there are minigames but they are also not interesting. One in particular really sucks, because you simply aren't given the information necessary to make the correct decisions, so you just click on random stuff until it somehow works.

It is one of those games where I suffered through the last 3 hours because I wanted to see the ending, but I had my head in my hands a couple times because it was just so annoying sometimes.

The writing.. well first of all, from a purely technical standpoint, it is bad. Clearly whoever wrote this is not fluent in english. There are tons of typos and grammatical errors all over the place. Things which could have easily been fixed by proofreading. Funnily, it gets better torwards the end. Or I just stopped paying attention, which is probably more likely.

From a stroy perspective, it is actually *ok*. Not great, not terrible. There were definitely some good parts, some twists, and some hateable characters. The main issue is that the gameplay is so boring that torwards the end you just use your mouse to scan over text really quickly to find hints, and stop actually reading it.

Overall score: meh/5.

Pixel hunt. You end up just compulsively clicking on every single word you see, just to see if it is a clue or not. Because otherwise you will get stuck for hours, not knowing that random information which you already knew is considered a "clue" by the system and mandatory to advance the game.

In the first case, you find out that the person you are investigating is running a company doing illegal activity. There are about 20 different lines of text telling you this, but only one of them actually counts as a "clue". This has a chilling effect which just causes you to compulsively click every single word that appears on the screen because you have no way of knowing what's a clue and what isn't. And I found that I spent more time clicking than actually reading. It became a game of pointless mechanics, just clicking words and moving words around.

review_text_raw:
The game really can't decide if it wants to be puzzly or hold your hand constantly, even artificially blocking your progression until it deems you "ready".

The UX is outright abyssmal, with every action having some sort of artificial delay, like waiting for some voice line to finish, or have an arbitrary fake progress bar go up. This will happen dozens and dozens of times. It can not be turned off. It can not be skipped.

It adds up to a LOT of time wasted, even if you aren't forced to repeat them because of the random minute "quizzes" the game occasionally throws at you, marking the only time where the game won't let you look up anything. You remember exactly WHERE the info would be, but no - you have to game over, retry, look it up, go through 1 or 2 minutes of unskippable very mediocre voiced lines again, and only THEN are you allowed to progress... to the next question. Rinse and repeat, unless you literally memorized every single little remark and detail from dozens of random conversations and social media posts.

The game ist just so incredibly tedious to play. It actively doesn't want you to have any fun. The story could be decent enough I guess, but it's certainly not enough of a payoff for the awful, awful gameplay.
